passage:
Daycare note, Toddler Room. Written by Rajni, caregiver.
Rehana (19 months) had a lovely moment today. A pigeon landed on the window ledge during snack time. I said, "Look, Rehana!" and turned my head towards it. She followed my eyes, spotted the bird and gasped. Then she pointed at it herself and looked back at me, checking that I had seen it too. We named it together: "Bird!" 🐦
Next step: I'll keep pointing out things around the room and wait for her to share her own finds.

qa.q: What landed on the window ledge during snack time?
qa.a: A pigeon landed on the window ledge.

qa.q: Why did Rehana look back at Rajni after pointing at the bird?
qa.a: She seemed to want to make sure Rajni was sharing the same exciting sight, enjoying it together.

qa.q: How could Rajni build on this at daycare?
qa.a: Rajni can keep pointing out interesting things and waiting for Rehana to point and share her own discoveries.

qa.q: What might it be like for Rajni when Rehana checks back with Rajni?
qa.a: It likely feels rewarding and warm, because the toddler is inviting Rajni into a shared moment.

grounding: It shows joint attention: a toddler following a caregiver's gaze and pointing to share focus.

passage:
Kunal carried Mridul on his hip along the edge of the mustard field. The yellow went on and on. Suddenly Kunal stopped and pointed at the neem tree. "Mridul, dekho! Mor!"
Mridul looked at his father's finger first, then followed it to the branch. A peacock was sitting there, its long tail hanging down. Mridul's mouth opened wide. He stretched his own arm out, pointed, and turned to his father's face.
"Haan, mor," Kunal said, smiling.
Mridul pointed again and bounced.

qa.q: Where was the peacock sitting?
qa.a: It was sitting on a branch of the neem tree.

qa.q: What does Mridul's bouncing and pointing again suggest he feels?
qa.a: It suggests he is excited and wants his father to keep sharing the discovery with him.

qa.q: What could Kunal try on their next walk to help Mridul learn from shared looking?
qa.a: He could point to other animals or plants, name them, and pause so Mridul can point first.

qa.q: How does Kunal seem to experience this moment?
qa.a: He seems pleased and connected, answering Mridul's point with a smile and the word for peacock.

grounding: It shows a toddler following a caregiver's pointing to share focus on an object in a rural setting.

passage:
At the market in Kumasi, Bilal held Kwame's hand while they waited for the bread. A man walked past carrying a stack of bright woven baskets on his head. Bilal gasped softly and looked up at them. Kwame watched Bilal's face, then twisted round to see where he was looking. He spotted the baskets and laughed.
"Baskets," Bilal said.
Kwame lifted his arm and pointed. "Ba!" He turned back to check Bilal was still looking.
"Yes, big baskets!"

qa.q: What was the man carrying on his head?
qa.a: He was carrying a stack of bright woven baskets.

qa.q: How can you tell Kwame wanted to share the sight with Bilal?
qa.a: After pointing he turned back to check Bilal was still looking, which shows he was excited and wanted them to look together.

qa.q: How could Bilal support this kind of shared looking?
qa.a: He can keep naming what they both look at and answer Kwame's points with words, like "Yes, big baskets!"

qa.q: If you were Bilal, what might you notice about Kwame's growth?
qa.a: You might notice he now follows your gaze and points back, a sign he is learning by sharing attention.

grounding: It shows joint attention: a toddler following an adult's gaze and pointing to share focus.

passage: I'm Jyoti from next door. Yesterday I watched Sangeeta, who is fourteen months old, on her mother's lap. Her mother pointed to the parrot on the wire and said, "Look, tota!" Sangeeta turned, followed the finger, and found the bird. Then she looked back at her mother's face and squealed, as if checking, "You see it too?" Her mother laughed and nodded. I can't know what Sangeeta was thinking, but they seemed to share that parrot.

qa.q: What did Sangeeta's mother point to?
qa.a: She pointed to the parrot on the wire and said, "Look, tota!"

qa.q: Why might Sangeeta have looked back at her mother's face?
qa.a: She seemed excited and eager to share the moment, checking that her mother was seeing the same bird, though Jyoti cannot be sure.

qa.q: How could a caregiver build on moments like this?
qa.a: Point to interesting things, name them, and wait for the child to look and look back, then respond warmly to what she noticed.

qa.q: What is it like for Sangeeta's mother when Sangeeta squeals and looks back?
qa.a: She seems delighted, laughing and nodding, enjoying the shared moment with her daughter.

grounding: A neighbour observes a toddler following her mother's point to a bird and looking back to share focus.

passage:
Monday: Rajni pointed at a crow on the balcony. Kalyani, one year old, stared at Rajni's finger, not the crow.

Thursday: Rajni pointed again and said, "Kalyani, crow!" This time Kalyani's eyes slid along the finger and landed on the bird. "Ah!"

Two weeks later: A plane roared overhead. Kalyani pointed up herself, then twisted round to see Rajni's face. Rajni looked up. "Yes, plane!" Kalyani bounced, clapping.

qa.q: What did Kalyani look at on Monday when Rajni pointed?
qa.a: She stared at Rajni's finger, not the crow.

qa.q: How can you tell Kalyani wanted to share the plane with Rajni?
qa.a: Kalyani pointed up and twisted round to see Rajni's face, then bounced and clapped with delight when Rajni looked too.

qa.q: What small habit of Rajni's helped Kalyani learn?
qa.a: She kept pointing at things, naming them and following Kalyani's own pointing, giving her many chances to practise shared looking.

qa.q: What would change if Rajni had not looked up when Kalyani pointed?
qa.a: Kalyani would miss the shared moment, and she might point less often if no one responded 😔

grounding: Shows a toddler progressing over weeks from looking at a pointing finger to following and then starting a point herself.
